pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Ray Diagrams & Images

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics, 'Light waves'):** "use of ray model to explain imaging in mirrors, the pinhole camera, the refraction of light and action of convex lens in focusing (qualitative)." The plane-mirror virtual-image construction and the qualitative convex-lens ray model sit at KS3; the FULL converging-lens ray-diagram construction with real/virtual + magnified/diminished + upright/inverted CLASSIFICATION, and the object-distance cases, extend into KS4 GCSE Physics (a natural KS3→KS4 bridge topic).

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no national PE):** NGSS has NO national performance expectation covering geometric-optics ray-diagram construction — it deliberately omits ray diagrams; the nearest MS framing is MS-PS4-2 (waves reflected/absorbed/transmitted, qualitative, NOT ray diagrams). Per Singh & Schunn (2016), optics ray-diagram content appears only in some US STATE standards (California, Rhode Island most directly), not the national PEs. So this topic is UK/international-curriculum-led; the US national anchor supplies only the reflect/transmit framing, and the ray-diagram skill itself is honestly UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Teach TWO standard constructions. PLANE MIRROR: image is virtual, upright, same-size, laterally inverted, equal distance behind. Construct by drawing two rays from a point on the object to the mirror, reflect each (angle in = angle out from the NORMAL), then extend the reflected rays BACK as DASHED lines — where they meet is the virtual image; the eye sees it along the reflected rays. CONVERGING (convex) LENS: use the three principal rays — (1) a ray parallel to the axis refracts through the far focal point, (2) a ray through the centre of the lens passes straight, (3) a ray through the near focal point emerges parallel — where they cross is the image. CLASSIFY by object position: beyond 2F → real, inverted, diminished (camera); between F and 2F → real, inverted, magnified (projector); inside F → virtual, upright, magnified (magnifying glass). REAL image = rays actually converge, can be caught on a screen, inverted; VIRTUAL image = rays only appear to diverge from it, cannot be projected, upright. Apply to the eye/glasses, camera, and projector.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/representational). Ray diagrams demand formal-operational, counterfactual reasoning ('where would the eye have to be?') and are documented as resistant even in college — so at 12–13 this is demanding threshold work. Success = independently constructing BOTH a plane-mirror virtual-image diagram AND a converging-lens diagram for a given object position, reading off real/virtual + orientation + size, and explaining a real device (why a camera image is inverted; why a magnifying glass is held close). Watch for rote-without-transfer: reciting 'equal distance behind' yet being unable to USE a diagram to answer whether moving back changes how much of yourself you see.
bestPractices: Make PREDICT–OBSERVE–RECONCILE the spine (Wosilait/McDermott): have pupils predict a striking outcome ('what happens to the image if you cover half the lens? if you remove the lens?'), observe it, then reconcile with a ray diagram — the conflict is what makes the diagram feel necessary rather than decorative.

Establish first that EVERY point on the object is a point source radiating light in all directions, and a ray diagram simply picks TWO convenient rays to locate one image point — this single idea dissolves both the 'cover half the lens = half the image' and 'triangular hole = triangular patch of light' errors.

Standardise the constructions as fixed routines: draw the mirror-normal / optical axis and mark F and 2F FIRST, then the plane-mirror two-ray + dashed-back method and the three principal lens rays, every time.
Use 'where must the eye be to see the image?' as a routine question (Goldberg & McDermott) so pupils tie the diagram to actually SEEING, not to a memorised distance rule.

Sweep the object from far to inside F and re-derive: the image flips from small-real-inverted to magnified-virtual-upright, so the three device cases (camera / projector / magnifier) all emerge from ONE construction rather than being memorised separately.

Do the hands-on optical bench FIRST — real converging lens + screen: catch the real image, then watch it VANISH when the lens is removed — so the diagram later explains a phenomenon the pupil has felt.
Concretise the abstract virtual image with a parallax analogy (billiards, Moore/Floyd/Thompson) to attack 'there is no image unless the object is directly in front of the mirror'.

Insist on the load-bearing conventions: SOLID rays = real light path, DASHED = virtual/apparent extension; a real image where solid rays cross, a virtual image where dashed extensions cross — the notation carries the real/virtual meaning.
keyRepresentations: Plane-mirror two-ray construction with reflected rays extended BACK as dashed lines to the virtual image (upright, equal distance behind).
Converging-lens principal-ray diagram: parallel-ray→far focus, centre-ray→straight, near-focus-ray→parallel, drawn on the optical axis with F and 2F marked.
The object-distance sweep (beyond 2F → at 2F → between F and 2F → at F → inside F) mapped to the real↔virtual, size, and orientation outcomes.
Optical bench / ray box with a real converging lens and screen — the physical apparatus the diagram models.

Device schematics tying each case to hardware: camera (beyond 2F: real, diminished, inverted), projector (between F and 2F: real, magnified, inverted), magnifying glass (inside F: virtual, magnified, upright).
The solid-vs-dashed ray convention itself (real light vs apparent path) as the notation that encodes whether the image is real or virtual.
commonMisconceptions: Rote-without-transfer: pupils recite 'the image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front' but cannot use a diagram to answer a real question, e.g. whether stepping back changes how much of themselves they see — the signature Goldberg & McDermott finding.

'Cover half the lens → get half the image' (and 'each part of the lens makes its own bit of the picture') — in fact the WHOLE image remains, just dimmer, because every part of the lens forms the whole image.
'Remove the lens → the image stays on the screen (maybe blurry), or becomes upright' — in fact the image disappears entirely; the lens is what makes the rays converge.

Line-of-sight misconception: an image can be seen only if it lies along the straight line of sight to the object, and it sits in different places for different observers — treating the mirror as a window rather than a reflecting surface.
'There is no image unless the object is directly in front of the mirror.'
Confusing real and virtual images: believing a virtual image can be caught on a screen, that a real image is 'inside' the lens/mirror, or that a plane-mirror image is real.
Drawing reasoning that silently violates the law of reflection, and measuring angles loosely from the surface/lens instead of from the normal/axis.
Confusing plane mirrors with curved/spherical mirrors, and believing a bigger mirror makes a bigger image.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–13 construct and interpret ray diagrams for plane mirrors and converging (convex) lenses, then classify the resulting image as real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished, and tie each case to a real device (camera, projector, magnifying glass). The spine is predict–observe–reconcile: pupils predict a striking outcome, observe it with real apparatus or a manipulable model, then reconcile it with a ray diagram so the diagram feels necessary rather than decorative. The load-bearing idea is that every point on an object radiates light in all directions and a ray diagram simply picks two convenient rays to locate one image point. Ray diagrams demand formal, counterfactual reasoning and are documented as resistant even in college, so at this age this is demanding threshold work; watch for rote-without-transfer.

activities.title: Catch it, then lose it: the real image on a screen
feedback: If a pupil expects the image to stay after removing the lens: the lens is what bends the rays together — with no lens, the rays from each point of the object keep spreading out and never meet again at one point, so the screen is just evenly lit and there is no image to catch.

If a pupil expects covering the bottom half to remove the bottom of the picture: every point of the object still sends light through the uncovered half, so the whole image remains — only dimmer because less light arrives.
If a pupil is surprised the image is upside-down: light from the top of the object crosses to below the axis, so a real image is inverted.
activities.rationale: Doing the hands-on observation first means the later diagram explains a phenomenon the pupil has already felt; the remove-lens and cover-half experiments directly confront the two commonest errors.
sourceClaims: Documented ray-diagram/optics misconceptions — rote-without-transfer on plane mirrors, 'cover half the lens = half image', 'remove lens = image stays', line-of-sight image, and inability to draw a ray diagram to reason — plus the effectiveness of predict-observe-reconcile / guided-inquiry explorations. Also: no NGSS national PE covers optics ray diagrams; only some US STATE standards (CA, RI) reference optics.
Seminal primary studies: students memorise plane-mirror rules without connecting them to real phenomena, and cannot apply converging-lens/real-image principles to an actual object-lens-screen system.
learnerActions: Set up a real converging lens, a bright object (e.g. a window or a lit arrow), and a screen on an optical bench or table.
Before moving anything, predict out loud: what will appear on the screen? Will it be upright or inverted, bigger or smaller?
Slide the screen until a sharp image forms; record whether it is inverted and how its size compares to the object.
Predict what happens if the lens is removed, then remove it and observe that the sharp image vanishes, leaving only a general patch of light on the screen (no image stays, and nothing flips upright).
Predict what happens if you cover half the lens with card, then do it and observe that the WHOLE image survives, just dimmer.
activities.intendedInsight: A real image forms where light rays actually converge, so it can be caught on a screen and is inverted; the lens is what makes the rays converge, and every part of the lens helps form the whole image.

activities.title: Construct the converging-lens diagram
feedback: If rays stop at the lens or pass straight through without bending: the lens refracts — use the two reliable rules (parallel ray bends through the far focus; the centre ray goes straight) so the rays converge.
If a pupil marks the image upright even though the rays cross below the axis: trace the ray from the object's top with a finger and see it land below the axis — that is why the image is inverted.

If an object inside F gives no crossing on the far side: the emerging rays diverge, so extend them backwards as dashed lines; where the dashes meet is the virtual, upright, magnified image a magnifying glass produces.
Treat drawn focal lengths as illustrative; focus on the ray rules and where rays cross rather than exact measured distances.
activities.rationale: Standardising the construction as a fixed routine (axis, F, 2F first, then the principal rays) builds the production skill that defines mastery, and sweeping the object inward re-derives the device cases from one construction.
learnerActions: On paper, draw the optical axis and mark the lens, the focal point F, and 2F on both sides first.
Draw an object arrow standing on the axis beyond 2F.

From the top of the object draw the three principal rays: (1) parallel to the axis, then refracting through the far focal point; (2) straight through the centre of the lens, undeviated; (3) through the near focal point, emerging parallel to the axis.
Mark the image where the refracted rays actually cross, draw the image arrow, and state whether it is real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished.

Repeat for an object between F and 2F, and for an object inside F — for the inside-F case the two reliable rays (parallel ray and centre ray) no longer cross on the far side, so extend them back as dashed lines to find the virtual image.
activities.intendedInsight: Where real refracted rays cross is a real, inverted image; for a converging lens with the object inside F the emerging rays diverge and must be traced back, and the crossing of those dashed extensions marks a virtual, upright, magnified image — all from one standard construction.

activities.title: Plane-mirror virtual image and 'where must the eye be?'
feedback: If a pupil thinks the image only exists when they look at the mirror straight on: view it from several positions (parallax) and trace the rays — the image stays at one fixed place behind the mirror whatever the viewing position, as long as reflected rays from the object can reach the eye.
If a pupil measures angles from the mirror surface: measure from the normal instead, or the reflection law is violated.
If a pupil can recite 'equal distance behind' but cannot answer the step-back question: return to the diagram and trace the rays that actually reach the eye.
activities.rationale: Tying the diagram to actually seeing, and probing with counterfactual 'where must the eye be' questions, attacks rote-without-transfer and the line-of-sight/window misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Documented ray-diagram/optics misconceptions — rote-without-transfer on plane mirrors, 'cover half the lens = half image', 'remove lens = image stays', line-of-sight image, and inability to draw a ray diagram to reason — plus the effectiveness of predict-observe-reconcile / guided-inquiry explorations. Also: no NGSS national PE covers optics ray diagrams; only some US STATE standards (CA, RI) reference optics.
Guided-inquiry billiards-parallax activity concretises the abstract virtual image and targets the 'no image unless directly in front of the mirror' belief.
learnerActions: Draw a plane mirror and an object point in front of it.
Draw two rays from the object point to the mirror and reflect each so the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the NORMAL (the line perpendicular to the mirror).
Extend the two reflected rays BACKWARDS as dashed lines behind the mirror; mark the virtual image where they meet.
Check that the image is upright, same-size, laterally inverted (left and right appear swapped), and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Mark an eye position and show that it sees the image by looking along the reflected rays; move the eye and discuss whether the image still exists and where it appears to be.
Use the question 'where would the eye have to be to see this?' and test a counterfactual, e.g. does stepping back change how much of yourself you can see in the mirror?
activities.intendedInsight: A plane-mirror image is virtual (formed by dashed back-extensions, cannot be caught on a screen), upright, same-size, laterally inverted, and equal distance behind; it exists whether or not you look straight at it, and the diagram — not a memorised distance rule — answers questions about what you can see.

activities.title: One construction, three devices
feedback: If a pupil names a device but cannot say why its image behaves as it does: go back to where the rays cross for that object position.
For the camera: the sensor plays the role of the screen; the captured image is inverted, and it is re-oriented afterwards (by the camera's processing or display).

If a pupil claims a wider lens makes a bigger image: separate image size (set by where the object is compared with the focal length, i.e. relative to F and 2F) from brightness (set by how much light the lens gathers, which depends on its width).
activities.rationale: Deriving the device cases from one object sweep prevents siloed memorisation and supports the required application to glasses, cameras, and projectors.
learnerActions: Lay out three object positions: beyond 2F, between F and 2F, and inside F.
For each, use the completed lens diagram to read off real/virtual, orientation, and size.
Match each case to its device: beyond 2F → camera (real, inverted, diminished); between F and 2F → projector (real, inverted, magnified); inside F → magnifying glass (virtual, upright, magnified).
Explain a real device using the diagram: why a camera's image on the sensor is inverted, and why a magnifying glass must be held close to the object.
Answer transfer questions, e.g. if the object moves from just outside F to just inside F, describe how the image changes.
activities.intendedInsight: The three familiar optical devices are not separate facts to memorise but different regions of a single object-distance sweep through one construction.

activities.title: Manipulable optical-bench model (optional dynamic scaffold)
feedback: If a pupil only watches and does not construct: use the draw-your-own-rays mode so the skill is produced, not just observed.
Live labelling of real/virtual and upright/inverted is a prompt to reason, not a substitute — pupils should still justify each label from the ray geometry.
activities.rationale: A manipulable model affords prediction-then-movement and built-in cover-half/remove-lens experiments; an existing geometric-optics simulation indicates such a tool is buildable. This is an optional dynamic scaffold — the paper construction skill remains the assessed objective.
sourceClaims: A geometric-optics sim with a draggable object, live principal rays, real/virtual image labelling, a screen, and cover-half/remove-lens experiments is buildable and effective.

Documented ray-diagram/optics misconceptions — rote-without-transfer on plane mirrors, 'cover half the lens = half image', 'remove lens = image stays', line-of-sight image, and inability to draw a ray diagram to reason — plus the effectiveness of predict-observe-reconcile / guided-inquiry explorations. Also: no NGSS national PE covers optics ray diagrams; only some US STATE standards (CA, RI) reference optics.
learnerActions: Using a draggable optical-bench model, drag the object arrow along the axis and watch the three principal rays redraw live and meet at the image (for a virtual image, it is their dashed backward extensions that meet).
Toggle a screen to try to catch the image, and notice that a real image lands on the screen while a virtual one refuses to project.
Use a shutter to cover half the lens and observe the image dim but stay whole; use a control to remove the lens and watch the image vanish.
Switch to plane-mirror mode and drag an eye position to test 'can I see the image from here?'.

Use a 'you draw the rays' mode where you place the principal rays yourself and the model checks them, then sweep the object inward towards F and watch the inverted real image grow larger and move farther from the lens as the object nears F, then become a large upright virtual image once the object is inside F.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the construction redraw as the object moves makes the covariation between object position and image properties concrete, and the built-in experiments make the key refutations immediate.

constraints: Mastery is demonstrated by independently DRAWING and CLASSIFYING both a plane-mirror and a converging-lens diagram, then reading off real/virtual + orientation + size and explaining a real device — recognition-only or multiple-choice tasks can consolidate and check rules but do not elicit the independent construction that defines the objective.

Keep the construction as a fixed routine: draw the axis/mirror-normal and mark F and 2F first, use the solid=real-light / dashed=apparent-extension convention consistently, and measure reflection angles from the normal and lens rays relative to the axis — not loosely from the surface.

A static annotated diagram or tap-to-reveal worked example is a useful reference and worked example but cannot let a pupil predict then move the object; use it as a companion, not the primary learning experience.

Ray diagrams are planar: the rays and axis lie in one plane. A 3D rendering of the flat construction tends to obscure the angles and crossing points; reserve any 3D treatment for an optional extension about capturing a depth scene onto a flat sensor/retina.
A device/persona framing (photographer, optician) can motivate application but cannot by itself build or verify the drawing-and-classifying skill.
Treat illustrated focal lengths as approximate; do not have learners rely on exact drawn distances.
This is demanding threshold work for 12–13: expect rote-without-transfer and plan to probe with counterfactual questions rather than accept recited rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the sources were not re-fetched. All retained sourceClaims are exact copies of the original row's sources[].claim strings.

Several legacy source claims are marked unverified in the row (Goldberg & McDermott 1986/1987 cited within a synthesis and not independently fetched; Moore/Floyd/Thompson billiards-parallax; PhET 'buildable and effective'). Claims of effectiveness should be treated as legacy confidence, not independently confirmed here; learner-facing text uses softened wording ('indicates such a tool is buildable').

The original strongly asserted a single interactive medium as 'ideal' and dismissed static images, 3D, and dialogue; these comparative/necessity claims are catalog preferences, not established efficacy findings, and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

sourceClaims for the 'Construct the converging-lens diagram' and 'One construction, three devices' activities are [] because the only candidate claim (KS3/KS4 curriculum placement) supports the topic's placement, not the specific pedagogical principles (fixed-routine production skill; one-sweep anti-siloing). The curriculum anchor still holds as context but is not evidence for those teaching moves.

Self-audit of physics content: remove-lens (image disappears) and cover-half (whole image, dimmer) are physically sound for a real image projected on a screen; a single converging-lens real image is inverted because rays from the object top cross below the axis; the plane-mirror image is virtual, upright, same-size, laterally inverted and equal distance behind. No arithmetic or force/motion content to correct.

The full object-position sweep in the original includes 'at 2F' (same-size real image) and 'at F' (no finite image / image at infinity); the activities foreground only the three device-aligned regions. Reviewers may add the at-2F and at-F markers if a complete sweep is required.

The camera explanation 'photo comes out the right way up even though the image on the sensor is inverted' is correct but the mechanism (sensor orientation plus electronic/processing re-orientation) is simplified in feedback; confirm the desired depth for this age.

probeDeeper: You said this image is inverted — trace me the single ray from the TOP of the object and show where it ends up.
If I moved the object to just OUTSIDE the focal point instead, what would change about the image — and how would the diagram look different?
What if the object were INSIDE the focal length (like an object under a magnifying glass) — would the rays still cross on the far side? Show me.
This is a camera lens. Point to what plays the part of the 'screen', and tell me why the photo comes out the right way up even though the image on the sensor is inverted.
assess.correctAnswer: The image is where the refracted rays actually cross (on the opposite side of the lens from the object): it is REAL (rays genuinely meet there, so it could be caught on a screen), INVERTED (the crossed rays put the image top below the axis), and — for an object beyond 2F — DIMINISHED. In the second diagram the child draws the parallel ray (refracting through the far focal point) and the ray straight through the lens centre, and marks the image where they cross.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats every image as REAL because it is 'on the diagram' — cannot distinguish an image formed where rays actually cross from one formed where they only appear to come from ('the image is real, it's right there where the lines meet').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two on screen and in a real bench setup: a real image catches on paper, a virtual one never does. Anchor 'real = rays actually arrive; virtual = your brain traces them back behind the mirror/lens'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is a real image because the rays are drawn meeting at that point on the diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a plane-mirror or diverging case the child still calls the image real and expects it to catch on a screen; asked 'could you photograph it there?' they say yes for a virtual image.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the image as UPRIGHT because 'the object is the right way up, so the image is too' — does not connect the crossing of rays to inversion.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace one ray from the object TOP with a finger and show it lands at the image BOTTOM. Reinforce with a real lens projecting an inverted image of a window on a wall.
errorPatterns.distractor: The image is upright because the object is upright.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Even with rays clearly crossing below the axis, the child marks the image arrow pointing up; asked why, says the object points up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes covering half the lens removes half the image ('cover the bottom, lose the bottom half of the picture').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do it live: mask half a lens projecting an image — the WHOLE image survives, just dimmer, because every point still sends rays through the uncovered half. Then re-draw showing multiple rays from one object point all reaching one image point.
errorPatterns.distractor: Covering the bottom half of the lens cuts off the bottom half of the image.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the translate task, asked what happens if the lower half of the lens is masked, the child erases half the image rather than dimming the whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: In the translate half, draws rays that STOP at the lens or continue straight through without bending — treats the lens as a window, not a refractor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the two standard rays as rules (parallel→through far focus; through-centre→undeviated) and have them practise on three object distances before interpreting again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child's own diagram has rays that never converge, so no image forms, yet they still mark an image position by guesswork.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot read real/virtual, orientation or size off the diagram; in the translate task draws rays that stop at the lens or don't converge, and locates the image by guessing.
responseLevels.full: Reads all three properties FROM the ray geometry and explains the causal link (rays truly meet → real & screenable; crossing → inverted), and transfers cleanly to a new case — re-draws for an object inside the focal length or explains a real device (camera/projector/glasses) using the same construction.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly identifies where the rays cross and can label the image real/inverted/diminished, but treats these as separate memorised facts — cannot say WHY crossing means real, or transfer to a new object distance (e.g. object inside F) without floundering.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a ray diagram of a converging lens with an object drawn well beyond the focal point. Two rays leave the top of the object, pass through the lens, and CROSS on the far side. Point to where the image forms and tell me three things about it — is it real or virtual, upright or inverted, bigger or smaller — and how the diagram tells you each one. Then take this second lens diagram, where I've only drawn the object and the lens, and YOU draw the two rays and mark the image.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting requires reading three separate facts off ONE construction — real/virtual from whether rays truly cross vs only appear to diverge, orientation from which side of the axis the crossing lands, size from the ray geometry — so a child who has only memorised 'lenses make things bigger' cannot fake it. The translate half (drawing rays on a fresh diagram) exposes whether they can PRODUCE the convention, not just recognise it: the classic failure is drawing rays that stop at the lens or bend the wrong way.
